Yes. Both the myeloid detrimental gene set and the lymphoid protective gene set show statistically significant positive within-set correlations across the multi-cohort sepsis population (N = 3,948 patients).

- Myeloid detrimental genes (35 genes, 595 pairs): mean pairwise r = 0.154, p = 2.75 × 10^{-33} (one-sample t-test), 69.2% of pairs positively correlated (sign test: p = 2.89 × 10^{-21}). The correlations are weak-to-moderate and driven primarily by neutrophil granule protein co-expression clusters (e.g., CEACAM8-LTF, OLFM4-LCN2).

- Lymphoid protective genes (49 genes, 1,176 pairs): mean pairwise r = 0.249, p = 1.71 × 10^{-112}, 72.9% of pairs positively correlated (sign test: p = 2.72 × 10^{-57}). The correlations are moderate and reflect the coordinated expression of TCR complex components (CD3E, CD3G, CD247) and T-cell signaling machinery (ZAP70, CAMK4, PLCG1, DYRK2).

The lymphoid protective gene set is significantly more coherent than the myeloid detrimental set (Welch t-test comparing the two correlation distributions: t = -6.13, p = 1.15 × 10^{-9}), consistent with the biological distinction between a tightly regulated adaptive immune program and a more heterogeneous, multi-faceted myeloid effector response in sepsis.
